# `study-repo` — the idea

Recorded 2026-08-17. A skill for the **`agent-workflows`** plugin, not the runner.

Proven by hand first: a subagent studied `testcase-validator` from ground truth and came
back with four key points, an ASCII diagram each, and eleven places its own docs contradict
its code. That run is the specification.

---

## 1. The skill

`gen-readme`'s Step 2 — *study the project from ground truth to find its key points* — is
the most valuable part of that skill and the part least specific to READMEs. It is currently
locked inside a unit that writes a README.

Pull it out and **run it in the background**, as a subagent.

Two reasons it belongs in a subagent rather than the main loop:

- **It reads a lot and returns a little.** Studying a repo means opening entry points, build
  files, schemas, routes, config. All of that lands in context and none of it is the answer.
  A subagent burns its own context and hands back the conclusion.
- **It is slow and independent.** Nothing in the session depends on it mid-flight, so it runs
  while other work continues.

Who consumes it: `gen-readme` (one diagram per key point), `review-tests` (*what does
passing prove* cannot be answered without knowing what the system does), and anyone arriving
cold at an unfamiliar repo.

## 2. The output is rows, not prose

The study returns a **table**, one row per key point, and a template defines the fields.
Prose invites an essay; fields force the study to answer the same questions every time and
make two studies comparable.

Draft field set, taken from what the `testcase-validator` run actually produced:

| Field | What it holds | Why it earns a column |
|---|---|---|
| **#** | Rank. #1 is the organizing idea | `gen-readme`: #1 is found before any feature list, and everything else is grounded in it |
| **Key point** | One line, concrete | This is what a reader remembers |
| **Ground truth** | The paths it was derived from | Makes the claim checkable. A row with no path is an impression |
| **Mechanism** | What actually happens, in the code's own names — real functions, routes, tables, types | *"a service talks to a database"* is not a finding. `store.rules()` at startup, `findViolations` per request, is |
| **Why it matters** | What a newcomer cannot understand without it | The test for whether the row belongs at all |
| **Diagram** | ASCII, one per row, mandatory | `gen-readme`'s count check: diagrams == rows. Fewer diagrams means a shorter list, never a skipped drawing |
| **Contradicts** | Any doc claim the code does not support | Fell out of the trial run and turned out to be the most valuable column — eleven hits in a repo that takes its ADRs seriously |

About three rows, four at most. Longer is an index, not a lead.

## 3. Reuse `reviewing-phrasing`'s reference pattern

`reviewing-phrasing` ships `reference/` — one file per document kind
(`readmes.md`, `design-docs.md`, `api-reference.md`, `test-plans.md`), each with a Contents
block, the structure that kind of document takes, and a review checklist.

That pattern is the template mechanism, already built and already shipping. `study-repo`
adds its field definitions the same way rather than inventing a second convention: the
fields, what each one must contain, and a checklist the study is held to before it returns.

It also means the two skills agree on what a document owes its reader, instead of drifting
apart.

## 4. It writes nothing. Anywhere.

**No file. Not in the repo, not in `tmp/`, not a cache.** The study is returned in the
message and lives only in the session.

This is the whole doctrine applied to the skill itself. A saved study is a document, a
document goes stale invisibly, and the next agent reads a description of a repo that has
since changed and believes it. The `testcase-validator` run is the proof: eleven
contradictions, every one of them a file that was true when it was written.

The study is cheap to reproduce and always current when reproduced. Persisting it trades
that for staleness and saves nothing worth having.

Consequences, accepted:

- Two sessions studying the same repo each pay for it. That is the price of never being
  wrong about it.
- Nothing to diff between studies — a *what changed since last time* would need a stored
  previous study, and that is the file this rule forbids.
- The session log holds it anyway, for whoever wants the history. A log is the record; a
  document is a claim.

## 5. Open

| # | Question | Lean |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Does `gen-readme` call `study-repo`, or do they stay independent and a person runs both? | Call it. Two units doing the same study differently is how they drift |
| 2 | Is `study-repo` the name? | Verb-noun, matches the spine. `map-repo` reads as producing an artifact, which is exactly what it must not do |
| 3 | Does the **Contradicts** column belong here, or in a separate doc-drift skill? | Here. It costs nothing once the code has been read, and separating it means reading the repo twice |
| 4 | How does a caller pass a focus — "study the write path", "study the test layer"? | An optional argument narrowing the study; with none, the whole repo |

  |  rule    -> rules.id        |   where enabled        collects ALL and refuses
  |  phrase  text               |   -> Map<int, string[]>  to start
  |  enabled boolean            |            |            |
  |  unique(rule, phrase)       |            v            v
  +-----------------------------+      folded into    RuleSets = {
                                       StoredRule       testCase:          Map<'name'|'summary'
  +-----------------------------+      .exceptions                        |'preconditions', Rule[]>
  | reference_documents         |                       referenceDocument: Map<'title'|'body',
  |  id text PK, title, body    |                                                Rule[]>
  +-----------------------------+                     }
       (content, not rules)                      ^^^^^ ONE Map entry == ONE "Rule Set"
                                                 A Field no Rule names has no entry.

                                           looksFor, flanked, reason, sorted(exceptions)]
                                          per rule, JSON'd, sorted, joined).slice(0,12)
     -- derived, never stored, never an operator's to type.

  Violation { field, rule, reason, text, offset }
     -- NO TABLE, NO FILE. Made per request by findViolations(), sent in the body,
        echoed to request.log.warn on writes only, and gone. This is why a Rule is

`default-rules.sql` writes the cross join of 74 Terms + 15 Symbols against the 5-row
`(content_kind, field)` values list = **445 rows**, `on conflict … do nothing`. It inserts
no `rule_exceptions`.

## #4 — One engine, opposite verdicts

| Field | |
|---|---|
| **Ground truth** | `src/app.ts` read routes, `src/violation.ts` |
| **Mechanism** | `findViolations` is reached from four routes. On a write, violations end the request at 422. On a read it is always 200 and the violations ride beside the content — and the content itself comes from TestLink over MCP for a test case, from Postgres for a reference document |
| **Why it matters** | The timing asymmetry falls out of it: edit a reference document and it is live on the next request; edit a rule and nothing happens until the process restarts |
| **Contradicts** | none beyond #2's |

```
                     findViolations(content, ruleSets)   src/violation.ts
                    /              |                  \
   bound.testCase  /               |                   \  bound.referenceDocument
                  /                |                    \
   WRITE ---------+        READ ---+                READ -+
                  |                |                      |
  POST .../test-cases     GET /test-cases/:id    GET /reference-documents/:id
  PUT  /test-cases/:id            |                       |
        |                         |                       |
  content came from        content came from       content came from
  the REQUEST BODY         TESTLINK                POSTGRES
                           read_test_case          select title, body
                           over MCP                from reference_documents
        |                         |                       |
        v                         v                       v
   violations > 0 ?          ALWAYS 200               ALWAYS 200
   YES -> 422                { testCase,              { document,
          nothing              violations,              violations,
          written              ruleSetVersion }         ruleSetVersion }
   NO  -> write through
          201 / 200          "refusing would put the content out of reach of the
                              caller who most needs to see what is wrong with it"

  UNCHECKED, served straight through (no Rule binds to them):
    GET  /projects                                  GET /reference-documents  (id+title
    GET  /projects/:projectId/suites?parentSuiteId=      only - a listing is how you find
    GET  /projects/:projectId/suites/:suiteId/test-cases  a document, not how you read it)
    POST/PUT/DELETE /projects, /projects/:id/suites/...
    DELETE /test-cases/:id
  -> these carry the Rule-Set-Version HEADER but no ruleSetVersion in the body:

  Timing asymmetry that falls out of this:
    edit reference_documents -> live on the very next request
    edit rules               -> nothing happens until the process is restarted
```

15 routes total in `src/app.ts`. There is no `GET /projects/:projectId` and no
`GET /projects/:projectId/suites/:suiteId`.

---

## Where the docs disagree with the code — all 11

**README.md**

1. *"Rule sets are appended rather than replaced… nothing in the API resolves a version back to its row"* — no rule-set row and no append-only table exist. Left over from the YAML-blob design removed in `49f783e`
2. *"A rule set is written under the content it checks, `testCase:` or `referenceDocument:`"* (line 311) — no such key; it is the `content_kind` **column**. The README's own SQL examples use the column correctly, so it contradicts itself
3. *"Test Cases, Test Suites and Projects can each be created, read, updated and deleted"* (line 8) — no read-one route for a project or suite. Line 293 is correct
4. *"Rules match terms… literally"* (line 213) understates two behaviours: a Term fires only where it `standsAsWord` (hyphen and underscore count as word characters, so `associates` leaves `re-associates` alone), and `matcherFor` rewrites whitespace runs to `\s+`, so a phrase matches across a line break. An Exception phrase is matched **without** the word-standing check, so it can suppress from inside a longer word where the identical Term would not have fired
5. The rule-set-version composition list (lines 244–246) omits `contentKind`, though it claims to be exhaustive and `ruleSetVersionOf` hashes it first
6. `npm run dev` cannot succeed from the walkthrough as written: `.env.example` ships `TESTLINK_API_KEY=` empty and `required('TESTLINK_API_KEY')` throws — after the no-enabled-rules check, so the reader hits an unwarned failure. The API-key step appears ~80 lines later
7. The README describes the vitest suite in detail but never gives the `npm test` command

**ADRs**

8. **ADR-0006** — *"YAML stays, as the storage format. Rule Sets are held as text in `rule_sets.source` and parsed at startup"*: false. No `rule_sets` table, no YAML in `src/`, `schema.sql` or the dependencies. ADR-0007 superseded it, but 0006 carries no supersession note (unlike 0005, which does)
9. **ADR-0001** — *"Rules are baked into the deployed image"*: false, they are read from Postgres. ADR-0004 flags this, so it is self-declared. There is also no deployed image — no Dockerfile
10. **ADR-0005** — *"How content reaches the database… there is one write path"* (`npm run load`): no such command exists. Carries its own superseded banner

**Other**

11. `default-rules.sql:26-27` says the file *"writes into all ten of them"*. There are five Fields and therefore five Rule Sets; README line 67 has it right

---

*All 225 tests pass (`npm test`), so the behaviour above is the behaviour that suite pins.*

Based on the search results, here's what I found about ISTQB test levels, test types, and their classifications:

## Test Types

Tests can be classified into four categories: Functional, Non-Functional, White-Box, and Change-Related Testing.

### Functional Testing
Functional testing should be conducted at every test level, although the objective of each level may vary. Functional testing is all about verifying the software's behaviour, focusing on the system's input and output and not on what's happening internally of that function or method.

### Non-Functional Testing
Non functional testing is performed at any level and is focused on how well the system or component not related to a functionality works such as reliability testing, portability testing, load testing, performance testing, stress testing, usability testing, maintainability. Non-functional testing may be performed at all test levels.

### Structural Testing
Structural testing is performed at any level and is based on analysis of the internal structure of the component of system like testing a menu structure and its structure coverage. Structural testing is a type suitable with component and integration testing and may be based upon the system architecture or hierarchy.

### Change-Related Testing
Changes are typically made to a component or system to either enhance it by adding a new feature or to fix it by removing a defect. Testing should then also include confirmation testing and regression testing.

Here are the search results for test categorization best practices regarding the testing pyramid in 2026:

## Test Pyramid Structure

According to the testing pyramid, the most tests are on the unit-level, fewer tests on the integration level and the least amount of tests on the system level. The three main categories are:

- **Unit Tests (Base)**: They check individual components, by themselves, ensuring each code unit works correctly as expected in isolation.

- **Integration Tests (Middle)**: They verify that different modules, services, or APIs work correctly together.

- **End-to-End Tests (Top)**: They simulate real user workflows to ensure the entire application functions as expected.

## Best Practices for Test Distribution

You should select carefully which functionality is tested on which level. If you can show a problem with a unit test, you use a unit test. Only if a problem cannot be shown with a unit test you go one level upwards by using an integration test or even a system test.

## 2026 Updates

In 2026, the testing pyramid is evolving. Modern teams are shifting toward a diamond shape. Unit tests remain the foundation, but E2E tests have grown in proportion. Teams using AI coding tools heavily are finding that a 60/25/15 ratio (or even 50/30/20 for high-stakes applications) delivers better incident rates than the classic 70/20/10.

Additionally, in the AI era, the recommendation is to run E2E tests for critical user flows on every PR merge, with the full E2E suite running nightly. Unit tests should run on every commit, and integration tests should run on every commit or PR.

Based on the search results, here's a comprehensive overview of Google's test size classification system:

## Test Size Classification

At Google, every test is classified into a size, with engineers encouraged to write the smallest possible test for a given piece of functionality. A test's size is determined not by its number of lines of code, but by how it runs, what it is allowed to do, and how many resources it consumes.

### Three Main Categories

**Small Tests:** Small tests run in a single process, and cover a single unit of code in a completely faked environment.

**Medium Tests:** Medium tests run on a single machine, and cover multiple and interacting units of code in a faked or real environment. Medium tests can span multiple processes, use threads, and can make blocking calls, including network calls, to localhost, but aren't allowed to make network calls to any system other than localhost.

**Large Tests:** Large tests run wherever they want, and cover any number of units of code in the actual production environment with real and not faked resources.

### Hermetic Testing

Tests are allowed to access a filesystem if they use a hermetic, in-memory implementation. To maintain reliability, medium tests should be hermetic (self-contained in setup, execution, and teardown), kept simple and clear, and written with caution to minimize nondeterminism.

### Test Distribution

Google recommends a mix of approximately 80% small tests, 15% medium-scoped integration tests, and 5% broad-scoped end-to-end tests.

Based on the search results, here's a comprehensive overview of the "don't mock what you don't own" principle and related testing best practices:

## Core Principle

"Don't Mock What You Don't Own" means that whenever you employ mock objects, you should use them to substitute your own objects and not third-party ones. The term originates in the London-school TDD community, the thrust of which is that test doubles should be primarily used to facilitate TDD to invent focused, usable interfaces between the thing you're testing and the code it will depend on.

## Why This Matters

If you use mocks/stubs as a design tool, introduced test doubles define a contract binding the client and the provider. In the case of external code, you, as the client representative, neither can define a new version of the contract nor cannot tweak the provider side.

The primary value of test doubles is design feedback, wherein any pain in faking something should be responded to not with ever-more-clever test double libraries, but with a redesign of the interaction between the subject and its dependencies.

## Recommended Approach

The recommended approach in such cases is not to mock things you don't control directly, but rather to wrap them in your own code, behind an interface, and mock that interface instead.

## Test Double Types

Mocks are the most commonly used form of test double, but there are many cases where Mocks perhaps are not the best choice and Fakes should be considered instead. A fake is a working, lightweight in-memory implementation of a dependency. Fakes are used for integration-style tests where you need to verify that your code works with a simplified version of a real system.

## Avoiding Over-Mocking

Test doubles should be used very sparingly as they all come with some drawbacks and the mere need for such tools is a smell for some bigger problems. Before adopting them, ask yourself: can I achieve the same results in any other way?

content.text:
Four axes, and they're routinely confused with each other:

| Axis | Categories | Defined by |
|---|---|---|
| **Level** (ISTQB) | unit → integration → system → acceptance | how much of the system is assembled |
| **Type** (ISTQB) | functional · non-functional · structural/white-box · change-related (confirmation + regression) | what question the test asks; applies at every level |
| **Size** (Google) | small = one process, fully faked · medium = one machine, localhost only · large = real resources, real environment | **what the test is allowed to touch** — not lines of code, not naming |
| **Doubles** | dummy · stub · fake · mock · spy | how much is substituted, and therefore what passing proves |

**Google's axis is the useful one for us.** A test's size is determined by how it runs and what resources it may reach — not by what it's called or which folder it sits in. # agent-runner — the flow

Drafted 2026-08-17. One process, not yet split into skills. Splitting is the last step, not
the first: a process cut into units before it works end to end produces units that hand each
other nothing.

---

## 1. The problem this exists for

**An agent writing tests produces coverage that is not coverage.**

`testcase-validator` is the case. 225 passing tests across 17 files, every helper commented,
`npm test` green. It reads as a well-protected system. It is not protected at all:

- every test runs in a single process with TestLink faked and Postgres emulated
- the two guarantees its own README names as mattering most — *that a write lands, and that
  the id it answers with is the id a read answers to* — are the two it never makes
- a 206-line hand-written fake stands in for TestLink, and nothing checks the fake matches it

The number is the trap. 225 is read as safety. What the 225 prove is that the code agrees
with fakes the same author wrote.

## 2. Test levels — ISTQB CTFL v4.0

| Level | What it tests | Test basis | Typical test object |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Component** (unit) | A single component in isolation, separately testable | detailed design, code, data model, component spec | components, units, modules, classes, data structures |
| **Component integration** | The interfaces and interactions *between* components | software design, sequence diagrams, interface and protocol specs | subsystems, databases, APIs, microservices, interfaces |
| **System** | The behaviour and capabilities of the whole system — end-to-end tasks, and non-functional characteristics | requirement specs, use cases, epics, user stories, state diagrams, manuals | the application, its configuration and config data |
| **System integration** | The system's interfaces to *other systems and external services* | system design, external interface definitions, workflows, protocol specs | the system plus the third parties it talks to |
| **Acceptance** | Validation and readiness for deployment — confidence rather than defect-finding | business processes, user requirements, regulations, contracts, installation procedures | the delivered system: UAT, operational, contractual/regulatory, alpha/beta |

## 3. Test types — ISTQB CTFL v4.0

| Type | The question it asks | Evaluates |
|---|---|---|
| **Functional** | *What* should it do? | The functions a component or system should perform — completeness, correctness, appropriateness |
| **Non-functional** | *How well* does it do it? | ISO 25010 characteristics: performance efficiency, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability, portability, flexibility, safety |
| **Black-box** | Does observable behaviour match the specification? | Derived from documentation external to the object — inputs and outputs, no internal reference |
| **White-box** | Is the internal structure exercised? | Derived from the implementation — code, architecture, workflows, data flows; measured as structural coverage |
| **Change-related** | Did the fix work, and did it break anything else? | *Confirmation* re-runs the failing case; *regression* hunts unintended effects in unchanged areas |

A type is not tied to a level. Every type can run at every level, which is why these are two
tables and not one.

## 4. The policy

### 4a. Component and component-integration tests do not count as coverage

They are still allowed to exist. They do not appear in the coverage matrix, and they never
answer *is this covered*.

The reason they are excluded rather than merely deprioritised: **a component test asserts
today's internal structure.** It is a restriction written down — the same failure mode as
the rule files stage 1 deleted, expressed in code instead of prose. When the structure
changes for a good reason, the test fails for no reason, and the change is what gets
questioned.

**Once the implementation is complete, recommend removing them.** They did their job during
construction — fast feedback while the shape was still moving. After that they are a brake.

*The cost, stated plainly:* component tests localise a failure to a line, and a system test
localises it to a system. Removing them trades debugging speed for freedom to refactor. That
is the trade being made deliberately, not an oversight — and it is only safe once
system-level coverage of the key points actually exists. Remove them before that and there
is nothing left.

### 4b. System, system-integration and acceptance tests are derived from key points

A key point describes a mechanism. A test at these levels exercises that mechanism through
the system's real entry point, against real dependencies. One key point, at least one test.

Worked from `testcase-validator`'s four key points
([testcase-validator-keypoints.md](./testcase-validator-keypoints.md)):

| Key point | Level | The test |
|---|---|---|
| #1 gate on the only path | System integration | Real Postgres, zero enabled rules → the server refuses to start. Then rules present → it starts and reports a version |
| #2 three refusals | System | Three requests produce 400, 422, 404 in their three shapes — and after the 422, TestLink is read back and holds nothing |
| #3 rule is a row | System integration | Write a rule row by SQL, restart, observe the rule-set version change and content that previously passed now rejected |
| #4 one engine, opposite verdicts | System | The same violating content: submitted → 422 and unwritten; read back → 200 with the violations beside it |
| the README's own gap | Acceptance | A write lands in a real TestLink, and the id the write answers with is the id a read answers to |

The last row is the one the existing 225 tests cannot make, and it is the acceptance
criterion the project itself wrote down.

### 4c. Functional by default; non-functional only when asked

Every derived test is functional unless the user asks otherwise. A non-functional test —
load, performance, security, usability — is a use case in its own right: it needs a stated
target, a stated environment and a stated threshold, and inventing those produces a test
that measures something nobody agreed to. So it is offered, never assumed.

## 5. When the flow starts — from the user's side

The trigger is not "the user asks for a test plan". It is the moment a person touches
anything that tests or runs the system:

> creates a test file · edits one · deletes one · reads one · asks what a test does ·
> adds or edits a CI workflow · asks for coverage · says the suite is green but something
> broke

At that moment, the offer: **run the analysis?** Not a report nobody asked for — one
question, and the process only proceeds on a yes.

## 6. The flow

```
   user touches a test or CI file — creates, edits, deletes, reads
   or says: "add a test", "is this covered", "the tests pass but it broke"
        |
        v
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │  OFFER: run the analysis?                   │   one question. no is an answer.
   └────────────────────┬────────────────────────┘
                        | yes
                        v
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ 1. STUDY the repo — background subagent     │   ground truth only; docs are claims.
   │    -> key points, ranked, #1 the organizer  │   returns rows, writes no file
   └────────────────────┬────────────────────────┘
                        v
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ 2. CLASSIFY every existing test             │   by what it is ALLOWED TO TOUCH,
   │      component / component-integration      │   never by its folder or its name
   │        -> DOES NOT COUNT                    │
   │      system / system-int / acceptance       │
   │        -> counts                            │
   └────────────────────┬────────────────────────┘
                        v
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ 3. COVERAGE MATRIX                          │
   │      key points  x  counting tests          │
   │                                             │
   │           #1    #2    #3    #4   README-gap │
   │   system   -     -     -     -       -      │   <- testcase-validator today:
   │   sys-int  -     -     -     -       -      │      225 tests, every cell empty
   │   accept   -     -     -     -       -      │
   └────────────────────┬────────────────────────┘
                        v
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ 4. REPORT — what passing proves             │   the verdict is a sentence,
   │    what it does not, one gap to close first │   not a percentage
   └────────────────────┬────────────────────────┘
                        v
              ┌─────────┴─────────┐
              | gap accepted?     |
              └─────────┬─────────┘
                        | yes
                        v
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ 5. WRITE the test                           │
   │      - at system level or above             │
   │      - derived from a named key point       │
   │      - in the framework the project uses    │
   │      - functional, unless asked otherwise   │
   │      - real dependencies; a substitution is │
   │        stated, never silent                 │
   └────────────────────┬────────────────────────┘
                        v
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ 6. RUN it — against the real thing, twice   │   once proves it passes.
   │    a test never seen failing for the right  │   twice proves it is idempotent
   │    reason has not been written yet          │
   └────────────────────┬────────────────────────┘
                        v
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ 7. PRUNE — only now                         │   component tests whose key point is
   │    list component tests that now only       │   covered above them. Recommend,
   │    restate structure. Recommend removal     │   show, delete on a yes. Never auto
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Step 7 comes last for a reason.** Pruning before step 6 removes the only tests there are.
The order is: prove the level above, then remove the brake — never the reverse.

## 7. What the flow refuses to do

- **Report a percentage.** Line coverage is what made 225 tests look like protection.
- **Count a test it cannot classify.** Unknown level is not "probably system".
- **Write a non-functional test nobody asked for.**
- **Delete anything on its own.** Step 7 recommends; a person answers.
- **Save the study or the matrix to a file.** Both are true only at the moment they are
  produced. They live in the session and in its log.

## 8. Open

| # | Question | Lean |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | How is level detected, given the folder name lies? | By what the test touches: does it import the real dependency, open a socket, reach a real database? Google's size axis, applied mechanically |
| 2 | Does the matrix have a column for "covered by a fake"? | Yes — that is where 225 tests land, and seeing them all in one column is the finding |
| 3 | Where does `cicd/` fit? | It is the runner for the system and acceptance rows where the project's own framework cannot reach them |
| 4 | When does this become skills, and how many? | After it has been run end to end on `testcase-validator` once |

# `study-repo` — the idea

Recorded 2026-08-17. A skill for the **`agent-workflows`** plugin, not the runner.

Proven by hand first: a subagent studied `testcase-validator` from ground truth and came
back with four key points, an ASCII diagram each, and eleven places its own docs contradict
its code. That run is the specification.

---

## 1. The skill

`gen-readme`'s Step 2 — *study the project from ground truth to find its key points* — is
the most valuable part of that skill and the part least specific to READMEs. It is currently
locked inside a unit that writes a README.

Pull it out and **run it in the background**, as a subagent.

Two reasons it belongs in a subagent rather than the main loop:

- **It reads a lot and returns a little.** Studying a repo means opening entry points, build
  files, schemas, routes, config. All of that lands in context and none of it is the answer.
  A subagent burns its own context and hands back the conclusion.
- **It is slow and independent.** Nothing in the session depends on it mid-flight, so it runs
  while other work continues.

Who consumes it: `gen-readme` (one diagram per key point), `review-tests` (*what does
passing prove* cannot be answered without knowing what the system does), and anyone arriving
cold at an unfamiliar repo.

## 2. The output is rows, not prose

The study returns a **table**, one row per key point, and a template defines the fields.
Prose invites an essay; fields force the study to answer the same questions every time and
make two studies comparable.

Draft field set, taken from what the `testcase-validator` run actually produced:

| Field | What it holds | Why it earns a column |
|---|---|---|
| **#** | Rank. #1 is the organizing idea | `gen-readme`: #1 is found before any feature list, and everything else is grounded in it |
| **Key point** | One line, concrete | This is what a reader remembers |
| **Ground truth** | The paths it was derived from | Makes the claim checkable. A row with no path is an impression |
| **Mechanism** | What actually happens, in the code's own names — real functions, routes, tables, types | *"a service talks to a database"* is not a finding. `store.rules()` at startup, `findViolations` per request, is |
| **Why it matters** | What a newcomer cannot understand without it | The test for whether the row belongs at all |
| **Diagram** | ASCII, one per row, mandatory | `gen-readme`'s count check: diagrams == rows. Fewer diagrams means a shorter list, never a skipped drawing |
| **Contradicts** | Any doc claim the code does not support | Fell out of the trial run and turned out to be the most valuable column — eleven hits in a repo that takes its ADRs seriously |

About three rows, four at most. Longer is an index, not a lead.

## 3. Reuse `reviewing-phrasing`'s reference pattern

`reviewing-phrasing` ships `reference/` — one file per document kind
(`readmes.md`, `design-docs.md`, `api-reference.md`, `test-plans.md`), each with a Contents
block, the structure that kind of document takes, and a review checklist.

That pattern is the template mechanism, already built and already shipping. `study-repo`
adds its field definitions the same way rather than inventing a second convention: the
fields, what each one must contain, and a checklist the study is held to before it returns.

It also means the two skills agree on what a document owes its reader, instead of drifting
apart.

## 4. It writes nothing. Anywhere.

**No file. Not in the repo, not in `tmp/`, not a cache.** The study is returned in the
message and lives only in the session.

This is the whole doctrine applied to the skill itself. A saved study is a document, a
document goes stale invisibly, and the next agent reads a description of a repo that has
since changed and believes it. The `testcase-validator` run is the proof: eleven
contradictions, every one of them a file that was true when it was written.

The study is cheap to reproduce and always current when reproduced. Persisting it trades
that for staleness and saves nothing worth having.

Consequences, accepted:

- Two sessions studying the same repo each pay for it. That is the price of never being
  wrong about it.
- Nothing to diff between studies — a *what changed since last time* would need a stored
  previous study, and that is the file this rule forbids.
- The session log holds it anyway, for whoever wants the history. A log is the record; a
  document is a claim.

## 5. Open

| # | Question | Lean |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Does `gen-readme` call `study-repo`, or do they stay independent and a person runs both? | Call it. Two units doing the same study differently is how they drift |
| 2 | Is `study-repo` the name? | Verb-noun, matches the spine. `map-repo` reads as producing an artifact, which is exactly what it must not do |
| 3 | Does the **Contradicts** column belong here, or in a separate doc-drift skill? | Here. It costs nothing once the code has been read, and separating it means reading the repo twice |
| 4 | How does a caller pass a focus — "study the write path", "study the test layer"? | An optional argument narrowing the study; with none, the whole repo |

You're right, and the error is specific: **I drew the flow in execution order, not in trigger order.** Study runs first when the process runs — but nobody ever types anything that would fire it. A skill with no trigger surface cannot be the head of anything.

Only one of the five has a trigger a person actually produces. That one is the starter; everything else is something it calls or offers.

| | Trigger a user actually produces | Can it start? |
|---|---|---|
| review-tests | edits/creates/reads a test file, edits CI, "is this covered", "green but it broke", "add a test" | **yes — the only one** |
| study | nobody says "study my repo" while editing a test | no. It's called |
| create | "add a test for X" — but that arrives *at* the starter | no. It's offered |
| prune | nobody asks to delete tests they don't know are redundant | no. It's recommended |
| remove-stale-runner-files | seeing a leftover file | separate trigger, separate skill |

Two consequences follow.

**Study stops being a skill.** If its only caller is the starter, it's a subagent the starter spawns — not a peer, not a unit, nothing in the menu. That also settles the question you answered "no" to a moment ago, in the same direction.

**The starter's name is now load-bearing**, and this is the one thing I'd push back on. `review-tests` reads as review-only. A user typing *"add a test for the write path"* is inside this skill's job, and a description that leads with "review" will under-trigger on it — the dominant failure mode. Either the description carries both wishes explicitly in its first line, or the name gets broader. `check-tests`, `test-coverage`, or just `tests`.

My recommendation: keep `review-tests` as the name — it's honest about what the skill *does* first, and every path starts by judging what's there — but write the `when_to_use` around the **file event and the wish**, never around the word "review". ## 9. The skill split — in trigger order

**Drawn by what fires it, not by what runs first.** Execution order and trigger order are
different diagrams, and only the second one decides what becomes a skill. A unit no user
phrasing reaches cannot be the head of anything, however early it runs.

Of everything in §6, exactly one has a trigger a person actually produces. That one is the
starter; the rest are called by it, offered by it, or carry their own separate door.

```
   ═══ the doors a user can open ══════════════════════════════════════

   edits a test file · creates one · reads one · deletes one
   edits a CI workflow · "is this covered" · "add a test for X"
   "the suite is green but it broke"
                    │
                    v
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  /agent-runner:review-test              THE STARTER              │
  │                                                                  │
  │   a. identify the wish — review? add? just editing?              │
  │   b. ( study )   PRIVATE. background subagent. no name in the    │
  │                  menu, no description in the system prompt,      │
  │                  reachable by nothing except this skill          │
  │   c. classify every test by what it touches                      │
  │   d. matrix, then the verdict                                    │
  │                                                                  │
  │   writes nothing. deletes nothing. ever.                         │
  └───────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘
                                  │ OFFERS. never runs either on its own
                ┌─────────────────┴─────────────────┐
                v                                   v
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ /agent-runner:create-test     │   │ /agent-runner:prune-test     │
  │                               │   │                              │
  │ system level or above, from   │   │ recommends removing          │
  │ one named key point, run      │   │ component tests now covered  │
  │ until it actually asserts     │   │ above them. deletes on a yes │
  │                               │   │                              │
  │ ALSO has its own door:        │   │ no door of its own — nobody  │
  │ "write a test for X"          │   │ asks to delete tests they do │
  │                               │   │ not know are redundant       │
  └───────────────────────────────┘   └──────────────────────────────┘

   ═══ a separate door, a separate trigger ════════════════════════════

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  /agent-runner:clean-runner                         MAINTAIN     │
  │  fires on meeting a file an earlier version of this toolkit      │
  │  placed, or on "clean up", "why are there two of these"          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

| Skill | Fires when the user… | Category | Exposed |
|---|---|---|---|
| `review-test` | touches a test or CI file, or asks anything about what the tests prove | ANALYSE — **the starter** | yes |
| `create-test` | is offered it after a verdict, **or** says "write a test for X" | CREATE | yes |
| `prune-test` | is offered it, once the level above is covered | PRUNE | yes |
| *(study)* | **never.** No phrasing a person types reaches it | STUDY | **no — private** |
| `clean-runner` | meets a leftover file, or asks for a cleanup | MAINTAIN | yes |

### Why study is not exposed

It is an internal function, and the class analogy holds. Three reasons it stays private:

- **No trigger surface.** Nobody says *"study my repo"* while editing a test. A skill that
  fires on nothing is not a skill.
- **Metadata is not free.** Every installed skill's name and description sit in the system
  prompt of every session. An unreachable one is pure cost, paid forever.
- **The caller owns the prompt.** `review-test` narrows the study to what it needs — the
  write path, the test layer, one subsystem. A skill boundary would freeze that prompt at
  whatever the general case looked like.

If a user wish for it does appear — *"explain this system"*, *"what does this repo do"* —
it gets exposed then, and named for the wish rather than the mechanism: `analyse-system`.
Not `study-repo`, which names what the toolkit does rather than what the user wanted.

### The naming rule

Prefix `/agent-runner:`, verb-noun, singular object, matching the sibling's spine
(`file-issue`, `take-issue`, `open-pr`). `review-test` · `create-test` · `prune-test` read

`scope-test` also gives it an honest user-facing trigger *inside* the set: *"what should we be testing here"*, *"where do I even start with tests"*, *"what's worth testing"* — questions people genuinely ask, and which no other unit answers.

Two different objects, no overlap, and the dependency between them readable from the names

```

`analysis-sut` is not an optional prelude. **What counts depends on the key points twice:**

| | |
|---|---|

attachment.snippet:
1	# agent-runner — the flow
2	
3	Drafted 2026-08-17. One process, not yet split into skills. Splitting is the last step, not
4	the first: a process cut into units before it works end to end produces units that hand each
5	other nothing.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## 1. The problem this exists for
10	
11	**An agent writing tests produces coverage that is not coverage.**
12	
13	`testcase-validator` is the case. 225 passing tests across 17 files, every helper commented,
14	`npm test` green. It reads as a well-protected system. It is not protected at all:
15	
16	- every test runs in a single process with TestLink faked and Postgres emulated
17	- the two guarantees its own README names as mattering most — *that a write lands, and that
18	  the id it answers with is the id a read answers to* — are the two it never makes
19	- a 206-line hand-written fake stands in for TestLink, and nothing checks the fake matches it
20	
21	The number is the trap. 225 is read as safety. What the 225 prove is that the code agrees
22	with fakes the same author wrote.
23	
24	## 2. Test levels — ISTQB CTFL v4.0
25	
26	| Level | What it tests | Test basis | Typical test object |
27	|---|---|---|---|
28	| **Component** (unit) | A single component in isolation, separately testable | detailed design, code, data model, component spec | components, units, modules, classes, data structures |
29	| **Component integration** | The interfaces and interactions *between* components | software design, sequence diagrams, interface and protocol specs | subsystems, databases, APIs, microservices, interfaces |
30	| **System** | The behaviour and capabilities of the whole system — end-to-end tasks, and non-functional characteristics | requirement specs, use cases, epics, user stories, state diagrams, manuals | the application, its configuration and config data |
31	| **System integration** | The system's interfaces to *other systems and external services* | system design, external interface definitions, workflows, protocol specs | the system plus the third parties it talks to |
32	| **Acceptance** | Validation and readiness for deployment — confidence rather than defect-finding | business processes, user requirements, regulations, contracts, installation procedures | the delivered system: UAT, operational, contractual/regulatory, alpha/beta |
33	
34	## 3. Test types — ISTQB CTFL v4.0
35	
36	| Type | The question it asks | Evaluates |
37	|---|---|---|
38	| **Functional** | *What* should it do? | The functions a component or system should perform — completeness, correctness, appropriateness |
39	| **Non-functional** | *How well* does it do it? | ISO 25010 characteristics: performance efficiency, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability, portability, flexibility, safety |
40	| **Black-box** | Does observable behaviour match the specification? | Derived from documentation external to the object — inputs and outputs, no internal reference |
41	| **White-box** | Is the internal structure exercised? | Derived from the implementation — code, architecture, workflows, data flows; measured as structural coverage |
42	| **Change-related** | Did the fix work, and did it break anything else? | *Confirmation* re-runs the failing case; *regression* hunts unintended effects in unchanged areas |
43	
44	A type is not tied to a level. Every type can run at every level, which is why these are two
45	tables and not one.
46	
47	## 4. The policy
48	
49	### 4a. Component and component-integration tests do not count as coverage
50	
51	They are still allowed to exist. They do not appear in the coverage matrix, and they never
52	answer *is this covered*.
53	
54	The reason they are excluded rather than merely deprioritised: **a component test asserts
55	today's internal structure.** It is a restriction written down — the same failure mode as
56	the rule files stage 1 deleted, expressed in code instead of prose. When the structure
57	changes for a good reason, the test fails for no reason, and the change is what gets
58	questioned.
59	
60	**Once the implementation is complete, recommend removing them.** They did their job during
61	construction — fast feedback while the shape was still moving. After that they are a brake.
62	
63	*The cost, stated plainly:* component tests localise a failure to a line, and a system test
64	localises it to a system. Removing them trades debugging speed for freedom to refactor. That
65	is the trade being made deliberately, not an oversight — and it is only safe once
66	system-level coverage of the key points actually exists. Remove them before that and there
67	is nothing left.
68	
69	### 4b. System, system-integration and acceptance tests are derived from key points
70	
71	A key point describes a mechanism. A test at these levels exercises that mechanism through
72	the system's real entry point, against real dependencies. One key point, at least one test.
73	
74	Worked from `testcase-validator`'s four key points
75	([testcase-validator-keypoints.md](./testcase-validator-keypoints.md)):
76	
77	| Key point | Level | The test |
78	|---|---|---|
79	| #1 gate on the only path | System integration | Real Postgres, zero enabled rules → the server refuses to start. Then rules present → it starts and reports a version |
80	| #2 three refusals | System | Three requests produce 400, 422, 404 in their three shapes — and after the 422, TestLink is read back and holds nothing |
81	| #3 rule is a row | System integration | Write a rule row by SQL, restart, observe the rule-set version change and content that previously passed now rejected |
82	| #4 one engine, opposite verdicts | System | The same violating content: submitted → 422 and unwritten; read back → 200 with the violations beside it |
83	| the README's own gap | Acceptance | A write lands in a real TestLink, and the id the write answers with is the id a read answers to |
84	
85	The last row is the one the existing 225 tests cannot make, and it is the acceptance
86	criterion the project itself wrote down.
87	
88	### 4c. Functional by default; non-functional only when asked
89	
90	Every derived test is functional unless the user asks otherwise. A non-functional test —
91	load, performance, security, usability — is a use case in its own right: it needs a stated
92	target, a stated environment and a stated threshold, and inventing those produces a test
93	that measures something nobody agreed to. So it is offered, never assumed.
94	
95	## 5. When the flow starts — from the user's side
96	
97	The trigger is not "the user asks for a test plan". It is the moment a person touches
98	anything that tests or runs the system:
99	
100	> creates a test file · edits one · deletes one · reads one · asks what a test does ·
101	> adds or edits a CI workflow · asks for coverage · says the suite is green but something
102	> broke
103	
104	At that moment, the offer: **run the analysis?** Not a report nobody asked for — one
105	question, and the process only proceeds on a yes.
106	
107	## 6. The flow
108	
109	```
110	╔═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
111	║  TRIGGER — the user's side, not the toolkit's                             ║
112	║                                                                           ║
113	║   creates a test file · edits one · deletes one · reads one               ║
114	║   adds or edits a CI workflow · "add a test for X" · "is this covered"    ║
115	║   "the suite is green but it broke" · "review the tests"                  ║
116	╚════════════════════════════════════╤══════════════════════════════════════╝
117	                                     v
118	                            ╱────────────────────╲
119	                            │ run the analysis?  │──── no ───┐
120	                            ╲────────┬───────────╱           │
121	                                     │ yes                   v
122	                                     │              do what was asked,
123	                                     │              say nothing further
124	                                     v
125	 ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

## What

Stage 2 of #102: rebuild the `agent-runner` plugin as five skills, replacing the six `qa-*`
commands and `setup-agent-runner` that stage 1 left with dangling references.

Quoted, from the session this was designed in:

> the major problem of agent writing test is lack of coverage. if you look into
> testcase-validator you will find out the 100, 200 test it mislead you are safe and
> protect. but it is not.

> we need to detect Level of test: the Component (unit), Component integration should not
> count to test. it sometime block code change. recommend remove once implement complete.

> the re-design focus on how user use skill. the key point is when-to-use.

This is the parent. The deliverables are split into child issues; this one holds the
reasoning they all resolve back to.

## Why

**A test count is read as safety and is not evidence of any.** `testcase-validator` is the
worked example: 225 passing tests across 17 files, every helper commented, `npm test` green,
and it proves almost nothing.

- Every test runs in a single process. TestLink is faked, Postgres is emulated by `pg-mem`
- A 206-line hand-written `StubTestLinkClient` reimplements TestLink — mints ids, enforces
  prefix confirmation on delete — and **nothing checks that the fake matches TestLink**
- `StubQueries` answers by matching substrings of the SQL it is handed, so a test asserts
  the store sends a string containing a substring the test itself chose
- The project's own README names the two guarantees the suite cannot make: *"that a write
  lands, and that the id it answers with is the id a read answers to"*. Those two are exactly
  the two untested

Size, tidiness and coverage percentage all fail to detect this. Only one question detects it:
**what does passing prove?**

**Three findings follow, and they shape every skill below.**

1. **What counts depends on what must be tested.** A test only counts if it reaches a key
   point. A system-level test exercising nothing on the list fills no cell. So the key points
   come first, always — a suite cannot be judged from the tests alone.
2. **Component and component-integration tests do not count as coverage.** They may exist,
   but they assert today's internal structure — a restriction written down, the same failure
   mode as the rule files stage 1 deleted, expressed in code instead of prose. Once the
   implementation is complete, recommend removing them.
3. **The trigger surface decides what becomes a skill.** Execution order and trigger order
   are different diagrams. A unit no user phrasing reaches cannot be the head of anything,
   however early it runs.

**Why a document cannot hold this.** Stage 1 deleted `docs/`, `.claude/rules/` and the
profile because a document goes stale invisibly and the cost lands on the agent that trusts
it. The same subagent run that produced this design found **11 places where
`testcase-validator`'s own README and ADRs contradict its code** — in a repo that takes its
documentation seriously. That is why the reasoning lives in the session log linked below and
not in a `docs/` file.

## Plan

Five skills. Two objects, deliberately: `analysis-sut` analyses the system **being** tested;
`review-ci-system` reviews the system **doing** the testing.

```
   /agent-runner:analysis-sut       what must be tested            the subject
   /agent-runner:review-ci-system   what the tests prove           the door
   /agent-runner:create-test        write what is missing          the work
   /agent-runner:prune-test         remove what no longer counts   the cleanup

   /agent-runner:clean-runner       the toolkit's own leavings — not about tests
```

The process they implement, reduced:

```
        what must be tested?
                 │              read the code, not the docs
                 v
        ┌─────────────────┐
        │   KEY POINTS    │
        └────────┬────────┘
                 v
        what do the tests prove?
                 │              classify each test by what it TOUCHES
                 v              only system level and above counts
        ┌─────────────────┐
        │   THE MATRIX    │     key points × counting tests
        └───┬─────────┬───┘     a join, not a step — and not a skill
            │         │
   what is missing?   what no longer counts?
            v         v
     ┌───────────┐  ┌─────────┐
     │  WRITE IT │  │  PRUNE  │
     └─────┬─────┘  └────┬────┘
           └──> back to <┘
             THE MATRIX
                  │  nothing left to fill, nothing left to remove
                  v
             ┌────────┐
             │ FINISH │
             └────────┘
```

Order of work, and it is forced by the dependency above:

1. `analysis-sut` — nothing downstream has rows without it → verify: run it on
   `testcase-validator`, and it returns the four key points already found
2. `review-ci-system` → verify: its matrix shows all 225 tests in one column and every cell
   empty
3. `create-test` → verify: the write-lands / id-round-trips pair, against a real TestLink
4. `prune-test` and `clean-runner`
5. Delete the six `qa-*` commands, `setup-agent-runner`, `audit-bind.ts`, `port-yaml.ts`
6. `CLAUDE.md` and `README.md` back, written from the code

## Expected outcome

An agent asked about tests in any repo answers *what passing proves*, not *how many tests
there are* — and the answer is derived from what the code does, never from a document
describing it.

## Done when

- [ ] The plugin ships five skills and no commands
- [ ] `analysis-sut` run against `testcase-validator` returns its key points
- [ ] `review-ci-system` run against `testcase-validator` reports every matrix cell empty
- [ ] One real test written and passing against a live TestLink and a live Postgres — the
      guarantee that project's README says its suite cannot make
- [ ] No `qa-*` command, no `setup-agent-runner`, no `audit-bind.ts`, no `port-yaml.ts`
- [ ] The session logs for this work are committed raw in `.sessions/`

## What's next

Child issues, one per skill, grouped under a milestone. Each cites this issue.

## Context

Session: `.sessions/724f5e90-d58a-4d96-84e6-dcee6f432d70.jsonl` — the whole design, unedited.
A snapshot; the session was live when copied.

The drafts written during it are carried on the work branch under `tmp/`:

- `tmp/agent-runner-flow-draft.md` — the flow, both ISTQB tables, the level policy, the skill
  split, and the naming decisions with every rejected candidate and its reason
- `tmp/testcase-validator-keypoints.md` — the worked example: four key points, four ASCII
  diagrams, and all 11 doc-vs-code contradictions
- `tmp/redesign-draft.md` — stage 1 and 2 inventory
- `tmp/study-repo-draft.md` — the study unit, before it was renamed and exposed

They inform. They do not bind: the code binds on what is true now.

## Out of scope

- `cicd/` and `.github/workflows/`, except where a deleted path breaks them
- Any change to the `agent-workflows` plugin — `analysis-sut` was considered for upstream and
  deliberately kept here
- A new install path. `make install` was retired in stage 1 and nothing needs it yet

gh issue create --milestone "$M" --label enhancement --label priority:high \
 --title "Delete the qa-* commands, setup-agent-runner, and the scripts that served the removed doc layer" --body-file - <<'EOF'
## What

Clear the ground before anything is written, so nothing new can cite something already dead.

- `plugins/agent-workflows-runner/commands/` — all six `qa-*`. Every one opens with an `@` include of a rules file stage 1 deleted, and resolves project values from a profile that no longer exists
- `plugins/agent-workflows-runner/skills/setup-agent-runner/` — it wrote profile sections and migrated forks. Both are gone; nothing survives to rename
- `cicd/tests/src/audit-bind.ts` and `cicd/tests/src/port-yaml.ts` — they served the markdown test-doc layer deleted in stage 1
- The `audit-bind` and `port-yaml` scripts in `cicd/tests/package.json`

## Done when

- [ ] The plugin directory holds only `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`
- [ ] `npm --prefix cicd/tests test` is still green
- [ ] `grep -rn 'qa-bind\|qa-plan\|qa-cases\|setup-agent-runner\|audit-bind\|port-yaml'` returns hits only inside `.sessions/`

Part of #104
EOF

gh issue create --milestone "$M" --label feature --label priority:high \
 --title "analysis-sut: key points from ground truth, returned as rows, saved nowhere" --body-file - <<'EOF'
## What

The first skill, and the one everything downstream needs — the matrix has no rows without it.

Studies a repo from **ground truth** (entry points, build files, schema, routes, config) in a background subagent. Existing docs are claims to verify, never the model. Returns about three key points ranked, #1 the organizing idea, one ASCII diagram each, plus every place the docs disagree with the code.

**It writes no file.** Not in the repo, not in `tmp/`. A saved study is a document, and a document goes stale invisibly — the trial run found 11 such contradictions in one repo. The study is cheap to reproduce and always current when reproduced.

Field template per row: `#` · key point · ground truth (paths) · mechanism (real names from the code) · why it matters · diagram · contradicts.

## Done when

- [ ] Run against `testcase-validator`, it returns the four key points already found: the validation gate on the only path to TestLink; the three-stage funnel with three refusals; rule-is-a-row / rule-set-is-a-Map-entry; one engine with opposite verdicts on read and write
- [ ] It writes no file anywhere
- [ ] `when_to_use` covers "what should we test here", "where do I start", and the internal call from `review-ci-system`

Part of #104
EOF

gh issue create --milestone "$M" --label feature --label priority:high \
 --title "review-ci-system: classify every test by what it touches, then say what passing proves" --body-file - <<'EOF'
## What

The door. Fires when someone touches a test or CI file, or asks anything about what the tests prove.

1. Get key points — from `analysis-sut`, or call it. There is no path that classifies without them
2. Classify every test **by what it is allowed to touch** — never by folder, never by name. Component and component-integration do not count. System, system-integration and acceptance count
3. Build the matrix: key points × counting tests
4. Report what passing proves and what it does not — a sentence, never a percentage. Name one gap as first

**Writes nothing. Deletes nothing. Ever.** A reviewer that can fix what it finds stops reporting honestly — it starts finding what it knows how to fix. It offers `create-test` and `prune-test`; it never runs them.

## Done when

- [ ] Run against `testcase-validator`, its matrix puts all 225 tests in the "behind a fake" column and every key-point cell empty
- [ ] It reports the two guarantees that project's README names as unmakeable by its suite
- [ ] It writes and deletes nothing

Part of #104
EOF

gh issue create --milestone "$M" --label feature --label priority:medium \
 --title "create-test: write at system level or above, and run it until it actually asserts something" --body-file - <<'EOF'
## What

Writes the test that fills a named matrix cell. Its own door is "write a test for X".

- System level or above — never a new component test
- Derived from **one named key point**
- In the framework the project already uses. `testcase-validator` runs vitest, so a new test there is a vitest file; a second test system beside a working one gives two answers to "did it pass"
- Functional unless the user asks otherwise. A non-functional test needs a stated target, environment and threshold — inventing those measures something nobody agreed to
- Real dependencies. Any substitution is stated, never silent
- Stable fixture names with reuse-or-create; no literal instance ids, no random or timestamp suffixes

Two loops before it is done: the test must have been **seen failing for the right reason** at least once, and it must pass **twice** against a fresh environment.

## Done when

- [ ] Writes and passes the acceptance pair `testcase-validator`'s README names — a write lands in a real TestLink, and the id the write answers with is the id a read answers to
- [ ] That test passes twice in a row against a fresh backend
- [ ] Breaking the code on purpose makes it fail

Part of #104
EOF

gh issue create --milestone "$M" --label feature --label priority:medium \
 --title "prune-test: remove component tests whose key point is now covered above them" --body-file - <<'EOF'
## What

Offered by `review-ci-system`, never triggered directly — nobody asks to delete tests they do not know are redundant.

A component test asserts today's internal structure. When the structure changes for a good reason the test fails for no reason, and the change is what gets questioned. Once the level above covers the same key point, the component test is a brake.

Shows every candidate by name, deletes on a yes, never automatically. A test the user chooses to keep is a decision, not a failure.

**Runs only after the level above is actually covered.** Pruning before that removes the only tests there are.

## Done when

- [ ] It refuses to run where no system-level test covers the key point in question
- [ ] It lists candidates and deletes only what the user confirmed
- [ ] The honest cost is stated when it recommends: component tests localise a failure to a line, system tests localise it to a system

Part of #104
EOF

gh issue create --milestone "$M" --label feature --label priority:low \
 --title "clean-runner: delete what earlier versions of this toolkit placed into a project" --body-file - <<'EOF'
## What

The runner's own cleanup, and the inverse of the setup skill it replaces: it only ever deletes.

Hunts what `make install` and the old plugin actually placed — `cicd/` installed and never used, `project-profile.md` sections this plugin wrote, `.claude/skills/agent-runner-flow/`, forked `qa-*` and `qw-*` commands, `docs/tests/` and its format contract, `templates/testcases/` copied into a project, `Makefile` targets calling a deleted script.

Boundary: remove only what this toolkit wrote, or what shadows what it ships. Anything untraceable is the project's — report it, leave it.

Named `clean-runner` deliberately, not `remove-stale-files`: the `agent-workflows` plugin already ships that name, and two skills sharing a name is the shadowing problem nothing announces.

## Done when

- [ ] Shows every file before touching one, and deletes only on a yes
- [ ] Adds no line to any file
- [ ] Safe to run twice
- [ ] Reports CLEAN when it finds nothing

Part of #104
EOF

gh issue create --milestone "$M" --label docs --label priority:low \
 --title "CLAUDE.md and README.md back, written from the code" --body-file - <<'EOF'
## What

Both were deleted in stage 1. They return only once the skills exist, so they describe what is rather than what was planned.

- `CLAUDE.md` — the four karpathy guidelines and nothing else. No workflow sections: the old §5 and §6 documented a pipeline that no longer exists. The retired `templates/CLAUDE.md` was exactly this file and is in git history
- `README.md` — generated from the code by `gen-readme`, then gated by `review-readme` plus the phrasing and typography reviews. The old one was 407 lines; the sibling repo's equivalent landed at 122

Also rewrite both manifests: `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` and `plugins/agent-workflows-runner/.claude-plugin/plugin.json` still describe `qa-*` commands and the profile.

## Done when

- [ ] No section names a unit that does not exist
- [ ] Every command, path and link in the README resolves
- [ ] One diagram per key point, SVG source committed alongside the rendered PNG
- [ ] The plugin loads from this tree with the new descriptions

Part of #104
EOF

---
name: review-ci-system
description: |
  Judges what a project's tests actually prove, rather than how many there are. Classifies
  every test by what it is allowed to touch, discards the levels that cannot answer
  "is this covered", and lays the rest against what the system must do — so a suite that is
  large, tidy and green is still reported as proving nothing when that is the truth. Writes
  no test and deletes none; it names the one gap worth closing and stops.
when_to_use: |
  Use whenever someone touches the machinery that tests or runs a project — creates a test
  file, edits one, reads one, deletes one, adds or edits a CI workflow — and whenever the
  question is what the tests are worth: "is this covered", "are these tests any good", "do
  the tests actually test anything", "the suite is green but it broke in production", "why
  did this ship broken", "review our test setup", "what's our coverage". Reach for it before
  writing a new test, because what to write is decided by what is missing, and before
  trusting a green suite, which is the case that never asks for review. Not for running the
  tests, and not for writing or deleting one.
argument-hint: "[path to the project, or nothing for the current repo]"
---

# Review what the tests prove

Target: $ARGUMENTS — the project under review, or this repo.

**A test count is read as safety and is not evidence of any.** A suite can be large, evenly
organised, carefully commented, and green, and still prove almost nothing — because
everything it touches is a fake the suite wrote itself. Size, tidiness and coverage
percentage cannot detect that. One question can:

> If every test passes, what is now known to work?

That is the only question this unit asks. Everything below is machinery for answering it
honestly.

## 1. Get the key points first

**A suite cannot be judged from the tests alone.** "Counts" has no meaning until something
says what the system must do — so the rows come before the cells, always.

Call `analysis-sut` and use what it returns: about three key points, ranked, #1 the
organizing idea. If the user has already produced them in this session, reuse those rather
than studying twice.

**Do not derive key points from the test names.** They describe what someone chose to test,
which is the thing under examination. Deriving the standard from the subject makes any suite
look complete.

## 2. Classify every test by what it is allowed to touch

**Never by folder. Never by name.** A directory called `integration/` full of tests that
mock every dependency contains no integration tests, and the name is what made that
invisible.

Read each test and answer one question: what real thing does it reach?

| Level | Reaches | Counts |
|---|---|---|
| Component (unit) | nothing real — single process, everything substituted | **no** |
| Component integration | other units, still all substituted | **no** |
| System | the assembled system through its real entry point | yes |
| System integration | the system plus real external services | yes |
| Acceptance | the delivered thing, as a user or operator meets it | yes |

**Why the first two do not count.** They are allowed to exist — but a component test asserts
today's internal structure, so when the structure changes for a good reason the test fails
for no reason, and the change is what gets questioned. It is a restriction written down. It
answers "did I break this refactor", never "does the system work".

**Level is only half the filter. The other half is relevance:** a test counts only if it
reaches a key point. A system-level test exercising something on nobody's list fills no cell.

## 3. Build the matrix

Key points as rows. Counting tests as cells. One extra column, and it is the one that does
the work:

```
                  #1     #2     #3     #4    the project's own
                                              stated gap
   system          ·      ·      ·      ·          ·
   system-int      ·      ·      ·      ·          ·
   acceptance      ·      ·      ·      ·          ·
   ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   behind a fake   225 tests land here, in one column
```

The last row is not a footnote. Seeing every test in it at once is usually the finding.

**Read the project's own admissions before judging.** READMEs, comments and ADRs often name
the gap outright — *"needed for the checks that suite cannot make"* — and a stated gap is
worth more than an inferred one. Quote it.

## 4. The verdict is a sentence, not a percentage

Say what passing proves. Then say what it does not. Then name **one** gap as the first worth
closing.

A percentage is what let a suite of 225 tests read as protection. Never produce one, and
never accept one as an answer.

Three findings that recur, each worth naming when it appears:

- **The oracle test.** An assertion that depends on a value the test supplied to a fake it
  wrote. That is the code agreeing with itself.
- **The second implementation.** A fake large enough to reimplement the dependency's
  behaviour — minting ids, enforcing rules — with nothing checking it matches the real thing.
  There is no contract test.
- **Islands.** Every test builds its own world, nothing is threaded, nothing is torn down —
  because nothing is real enough to leak.

## 5. Offer. Never run

This unit **writes nothing and deletes nothing, ever.** A reviewer able to fix what it finds
stops reporting honestly: it starts finding what it knows how to fix.

Two offers, and both stop for a person:

- a gap worth closing → `create-test`
- component tests whose key point is now covered above them → `prune-test`, and only once
  that cover actually exists

## Worked example

`testcase-validator`: 225 passing tests across 17 files, every helper commented, `npm test`
green.

Classified: every test runs in a single process with TestLink faked and Postgres emulated by
`pg-mem`. All 225 land in *behind a fake*. Every key-point cell is empty.

Its own README names the two guarantees its suite cannot make — *that a write lands, and that
the id it answers with is the id a read answers to*. Those two are exactly the two untested.

Verdict: **the suite proves the code agrees with fakes the same author wrote.** It does not
prove a write reaches TestLink. First gap: the acceptance pair the README already names.

## Steps

Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:

    Task Progress:
    - [ ] Key points obtained — from analysis-sut, never from the test names
    - [ ] Every test classified by what it reaches, not by where it lives
    - [ ] Matrix built, with the behind-a-fake column filled in
    - [ ] The project's own stated gaps read and quoted
    - [ ] Verdict written as a sentence; no percentage anywhere
    - [ ] One gap named as first
    - [ ] Offered create-test or prune-test; ran neither

## Report

Two lines and a question:

    REVIEWED — 225 tests, every one behind a fake. Nothing proves a write reaches TestLink.
    Next: close the acceptance pair the README already names.
    Want the matrix?

A suite that does prove something reads the same way:

    REVIEWED — 12 of 14 key-point cells filled. #3 has no system-level test.
    Next: cover #3, or accept the gap.

And a refusal is a verdict too:

    NOT REVIEWED — no key points; analysis-sut could not read this repo from ground truth.
    Next: say what this system is meant to do, and I will classify against that.

The matrix, the per-test classification and the findings are prepared and held until asked.
